newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam premier said to oppose new auto ventures.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam premier said to oppose new auto ventures.

text.p: Hyundai Motor Corp's plan for an automotive joint venture in Vietnam is opposed by Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet, who feels the market is already crowded by too many carmakers, a senior government official said on Monday.
"I know that the prime minister is not in favour of the Hyundai project, he wants to decline it," Vice-Minister for Industry Nguyen Xuan Chuan told Reuters by telephone.
"He's saying that 14 licences is too many now," he added.

Chuan said government ministries were trying to persuade Kiet to approve the South Korean industrial giant's project, which would take the number of licences issued to foreign vehicle makers in Vietnam to 15.
Lee Jun-ha, a manager at Hyundai's public information department in South Korea, said the venture was still on.
"We don't believe the remarks were the Vietnamese government's official stance," he said.
A senior official in the Ministry of Planning and Investment said last month that approval for the $250 million project with the Interior Ministry would be granted before the end of 1996.
Some manufacturers have complained that too many licences have been approved for a market in which just 39,800 vehicles were sold in 1995.
Chrysler Corp is reviewing plans to open a $192 million assembly plant near Ho Chi Minh City because the field has been opened to so many competitors.
Vice-minister Chuan, who is responsible for auto industry policy, said there was no need to limit the number of foreign joint ventures because the market is set to expand.

He told a recent industry conference that if demand contined to exceed projections at its present rate, the market could stand at 105,000 units sold annually by 2005, more than 2.5 times its current size and equivalent to 77 percent of production capacity.

Chuan said the government should grant a licence to "anybody who is willing to meet" an official requirement that carmakers produce a share -- 30 percent after 10 years of operation -- of their components locally.
Manufacturers complain less about the rule on locally produced parts than they do about strict quotas for imports of unassembled vehicles, known as complete knockdown kits (CKDs).
Last year's car CKD import quota was 6,000, a tiny number which had to be shared between the half-dozen plants now operating with an estimated combined capacity of some 30,000 units a year.
Chuan has been urging the government to scrap CKD quotas, which often leave plants idle for long periods.
The government-run weekly magazine Vietnam Investment Review said Hyundai was considering a number of new projects that would push its investment in Vietnam to about $700 million.
